title: RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Abstract claims 'efficient constant-time retrieval and fusion for all graph sizes,' but Section 3.1 explicitly states that retrieval complexity is O(log N) ('guarantees efficient O(log_2 N) end-to-end retrieval and fusion time'), which is logarithmic, not constant-time.

Abstract claims 'achieving near-perfect accuracy in all tested scenarios,' but the highest reported accuracy in the paper is 87.34% (Table 2, GLEM+RAG4GFM on Computers). No result reaches a level that could be considered near-perfect (e.g., >98%).

Text states 'GLEM+RAG4GFM achieves 83.12% accuracy on node classification in the Computers dataset, representing a relative gain of approximately 5.5% over GLEM.' Table 2 shows GLEM+RAG4GFM accuracy on Computers is 87.34%, not 83.12%. The 83.12% figure is inconsistent with the table, and the 5.5% relative gain is also incorrect against either value.

Text says 'GraphGPT+RAG4GFM attains 60.37% accuracy on link prediction, outperforming its vanilla counterpart by 5.1%.' Table 2 shows GraphGPT link prediction accuracy on Computers is 54.27 and GraphGPT+RAG4GFM is 60.37. The absolute difference is 6.1 percentage points, and the relative improvement is ~11.2%. Neither the absolute nor relative improvement matches 5.1%.

Figure 3 reports link prediction accuracy on History for AnyGraph+RAG4GFM as 63.5, but Table 2 (link prediction section) shows AnyGraph+RAG4GFM accuracy on History as 41.74. These numbers differ by over 20 points, indicating fabricated or inconsistent data between the ablation and the main experimental results.

Text claims 'retrieval is by far the most critical component, accounting for over 80% of RAG4GFM's performance gains.' The ablation compares full RAG4GFM (79.6) to w/o RAG (73.5), but w/o RAG removes the entire RAG pipeline, not just the retrieval module. The 80% attribution is an overstatement that conflates the entire RAG framework with a single component; component-level ablation shows other components (fusion, indexing) also contribute significantly.

The table compares GraphLoRA (a parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning method for LLMs [22]) against RAG4GFM applied to AnyGraph (a GNN‑based GFM). GraphLoRA is not designed for GNN backbones, making the baseline inappropriate. Additionally, the time metric is ambiguous (training hours vs. inference retrieval time), and no per‑query latency or test‑set scale is reported, which renders the comparison unfair and unreproducible.

Conclusion claims evaluation 'across all possible graph domains and tasks.' The experiments cover only six task types and a limited set of datasets; the claim is a gross exaggeration not supported by the reported scope.
